title: I built an AI RPG where the LLM isn't allowed to control the game state. Has anyone else tried this?
author: -TheFlea-
selftext:
I built an AI RPG where the LLM is not allowed to control the game state. Has anyone else tried this architecture?

Most AI RPG implementations I've seen seem to give the language model enormous authority: it receives the current situation, generates what happens next, and the generated narrative effectively becomes reality.

I went in the opposite direction.

I built a playable RPG where the LLM is primarily an interpreter and narrator operating around a separate canonical game state.

The basic rule is:

The model can describe reality. It cannot simply make reality true by saying it.

Player input arrives as unrestricted natural language. The system has to distinguish between what the player actually authorized and things the model might merely infer.

For example:

“I look around for somebody who might be hiring.”

does not authorize:

\- approaching somebody

\- starting a conversation

\- accepting work

\- traveling somewhere

\- deciding how the player character feels

The world state, NPC knowledge, relationships, time, money, resources and consequences persist separately from the prose.

NPCs also have bounded knowledge and their own state rather than automatically knowing whatever the narrator knows.

Uncertainty is resolved separately as well, so the narrator can't simply choose the outcome that produces the nicest story.

The difficult part has been making all of that work while still allowing the player to type essentially arbitrary actions rather than selecting from a predetermined menu.

I am not a programmer by training. I designed the system and used AI coding tools heavily to implement it. The first playable version is now running.

What I'm trying to understand is whether other people working with LLMs in games have converged on a similar separation between:

semantic interpretation → canonical state → resolution → narration

rather than letting the LLM itself function as the source of truth.

Has anyone here built or experimented with something similar?

comments.author: SurvivalHermit
comments.body: I have felt for a while that we sort of went too far with LLM's when they first came out. Wanting to offload the entire game engine (in ttrpgs and in video games) to LLM's to create truly unique experiences. As of right now they are just not able to do that. context limits and the degradation of continuity over time is a huge hurdle. Something AI can be good at is taking in telemetry data and outputting a narrative based on that data. I truly think that SpacetimeDB accidentally made the most AI friendly server architecture. Allowing the AI to have limited ability to manipulate DB values (within bounded parameters) to affect real time narrative driven change to a play space is I think where we are at right now.

replies.author: -TheFlea-
replies.body:
This is very close to the conclusion I ended up at.

The breakthrough for me was realizing the LLM shouldn't be the game engine, and it shouldn't own canonical truth. I use it primarily as a semantic interpreter/narrator operating against persistent server-side state.

The server owns what is actually true: time, location, material state, NPC state/knowledge, relationships, consequences, etc. The LLM can interpret what the player is trying to do and propose changes, but it doesn't get to simply declare that those changes happened. They have to pass through bounded authority before becoming canonical.

That also changes the context-window problem quite a bit. The model doesn't have to remember the world indefinitely because the world remembers itself. Each turn it gets the relevant slice of canonical reality rather than being asked to reconstruct continuity from conversation history.

I'm increasingly convinced the useful role for LLMs in games isn't "generate an entire game." It's putting a semantic layer between a human being and a persistent simulation.

replies.author: SurvivalHermit
replies.body:
I agree. One of the great things about TTRPGs is its the only game where natural language is an input to the game. You literally say anything and the GM can turn that into game relevant action. LLM's give us the ability to use this in digital games as well whiteout the use of a human GM.

I actually made a game for my stream before i stopped streaming where they were given scrabble tiles as rewards for the amount of time they watched. They could then use these tiles to make any word they wanted to "attack" the boss. An LLM matched that natural language to the closest hard coded "skill" of the chat character and executed that attack. So instead of just typing "punch" over and over again to use the punch attack a viewer could type "uppercut" if they had the letters and still execute the punch skill. The damage calculation was tied to the letter scores of the tiles so you were encouraged to use creative words. 

Natural language interpretation and creating narrative out of data is an LLM super power and it is 100% where the future of gaming is.

comments.author: Hanksdaddy
comments.body: I had a similar idea but the further I worked through it the more it dawned on me that for it to really work as a game you have to take away anything interesting ai might do and demote it to a chatbot/narrarator which ends up not really being fun. The promise of using ai in games is real intelligence, NPCs with “real” lives and motivations, player freedom to find an interesting thread no one anticipated and pull it as far as it can go. Smarter folks than me might figure out how to do that but at least right now I don’t think the tech supports it

replies.author: -TheFlea-
replies.body:
I get what your saying the way I handled it was to have the llm interpret player inputs semanticly...feed that to the server for verification around know world state facts ect. Then it narrates back to the player...the llm then cannot violate reality in game ....of course the world is dynamic...think osr gaming from the 70s ....the Best original rpgs used a human gm that would do both of these tasks simultaneously....problems with bookkeeping of course...endless charts and ledgers and skill and npc ect.
So what if the server computes all ledgers skills world state facts ect.
The next issue with the human gm is the cognitive bandwidth to hold together the creative story...that's where the llm comes in
Both together present the world and evolving story back to the player
Uncertainty is answered by an oracle
You can attempt anything and the world around you will answer according to risk and your skills inventory ect.
Npcs are tracked and affected by the world in much the same way...so now my interactions with the are very dynamic as they have there own lives pressures and memories of events...

comments.author: Evoroth
comments.body:
Yeah,  this is the pattern that's actually held up for me: the LLM proposes, the sim disposes. A few things that made it robust:

\- Treat the model's output as a request, not an effect. It emits a structured intent (action + target + params), the server validates it against canonical state, and only then does anything change. Freeform prose in, structured intent out.

\- Keep a strict allow-list of verbs it can even propose. "Look for someone hiring" can surface candidates, but approach / accept work / travel are separate authorized actions, which is the line you're already drawing.

\- Give NPCs their own knowledge scope and pass the model only that slice each turn. Fixes bounded knowledge and most of the context bloat, since the world remembers itself.

Keeping resolution separate from narration is the big one. The moment the narrator can pick the outcome that makes the nicest story, consistency dies, etc. Sounds like you've already landed there.

comments.author: Lavio00
comments.body:
You are essentially explaining something a lot of vibecoders are slowly creating a consensus around. We give the bots way too much authority at each incremental step, which leads it to make completely baseless assumption on design- and execution intent. Then we scratch our head and get frustrated, yellong at the llm (which, ofc, bows deeply and begs for forgivness).

Truly efficient workflows (whether in your game or in general software dev by way of vibecoding) will come down to if you can remove the flamethrower-nozzle of these models, and turn it into a laser. Pinpoint accurate decisions at every incremental step. But that’s only possible with the correct constitution, modularity and orchestration. 

Basically all that yapping for me just to say: real efficient vibecoding will come down to how you can line up everything *before* the first line of code is written.
